title: Upper Density
content:
The **upper density** of A ⊆ ℕ is:

d̄(A) = limsup_{n→∞} |A ∩ [1,n]| / n

This measures the 'proportion' of naturals in A, taking the limsup to capture asymptotic behavior even when the limit doesn't exist.
mathContext: Axiomatized as a function Set ℕ → ℝ. The exact definition requires filter-theoretic machinery (limsup over atTop filter).

title: Lower Density
content:
The **lower density** is:

d̲(A) = liminf_{n→∞} |A ∩ [1,n]| / n

When d̄(A) = d̲(A), the set has a well-defined **natural density**.

title: Positive Upper Density
content:
A set has **positive upper density** if d̄(A) > 0.

This is the key hypothesis in Erdős's conjecture. Examples:
- Even numbers: d̄ = 1/2
- Primes: d̄ = 0 (too sparse!)
- {1, 2, ..., n, 2n, 2n+1, ..., 3n, ...}: d̄ = 1/2 but d̲ = 0

title: Density Bounds
content:
For any A ⊆ ℕ:

0 ≤ d̲(A) ≤ d̄(A) ≤ 1

The bounds follow from the definition: |A ∩ [1,n]| / n is always in [0,1].

title: Sumset
content:
The **sumset** B + B consists of all pairwise sums:

B + B = {b₁ + b₂ : b₁, b₂ ∈ B}

For finite B = {1, 2, 3}, we get B + B = {2, 3, 4, 5, 6}.

For infinite B, the sumset is always infinite and has positive density.
mathContext: Defined as a set comprehension: {n | ∃ b₁ b₂, b₁ ∈ B ∧ b₂ ∈ B ∧ n = b₁ + b₂}

title: Shifted Sumset
mathContext: $B + B + t = \{(b_1 : \mathbb{Z}) + b_2 + t \mid b_1, b_2 \in B\}$, with $t \in \mathbb{Z}$

title: Finite Sums Set
content:
The **finite sums set** FS(B) consists of all sums of distinct elements:

FS(B) = {Σᵢ∈I bᵢ : I finite nonempty, elements distinct}

For B = {1, 2, 4}, FS(B) = {1, 2, 4, 3, 5, 6, 7}.

This is much larger than B + B since it includes sums of any number of terms.
mathContext: $\text{FS}(B) = \{\sum_{i \in I} b_i \mid I \subseteq B \text{ finite nonempty}\}$

title: Coloring
content:
A **k-coloring** of ℕ is a function c : ℕ → Fin k.

In Ramsey theory, we ask: given any coloring, must some structure be monochromatic?

title: Monochromatic Set
content:
A set S is **monochromatic** under coloring c if all elements have the same color:

∃ color, ∀ n ∈ S, c(n) = color

Hindman's theorem guarantees monochromatic FS(B).

title: Hindman's Theorem
content:
**Hindman's Theorem (1974):**

For any finite coloring of ℕ, there exists an infinite set B such that FS(B) is monochromatic.

This is a cornerstone of Ramsey theory. The original proof was combinatorial (86 pages!); Furstenberg later gave an ergodic-theoretic proof.
mathContext: Axiomatized as hindman_theorem. The proof requires sophisticated techniques from either combinatorics or dynamics.

title: The Erdős Conjecture
content:
**Erdős's Conjecture (1975):**

If A ⊆ ℕ has positive upper density, then there exists an infinite B ⊆ ℕ and integer t such that B + B + t ⊆ A.

This is a 'density version' of Hindman: instead of coloring, use density > 0.

Note: We only get B + B + t, not all of FS(B). The density condition is weaker than 'one color class', so we get a weaker conclusion.
mathContext: $\bar{d}(A) > 0 \Rightarrow \exists B \subseteq \mathbb{N}$ infinite, $\exists t \in \mathbb{Z}: B + B + t \subseteq A$, where $B + B = \{b_1 + b_2 : b_1, b_2 \in B\}$.

title: Kra-Moreira-Richter-Robertson Theorem
content:
**The Erdős Conjecture is TRUE!**

Proved by Kra, Moreira, Richter, and Robertson in 2024.

The proof uses:
1. Furstenberg correspondence (density → measure)
2. Ergodic theory on nilmanifolds
3. Structure theory for dynamical systems

Reference: 'A proof of Erdős's B+B+t conjecture', Commun. Am. Math. Soc. (2024)
mathContext: Axiomatized as `kra_moreira_richter_robertson : ErdosConjecture656`. The proof relies on Host-Kra structure theory for $\mathbb{Z}$-actions.

title: High Density Case
content:
**High Density Simplification:**

If d̄(A) > 1/2, then we can take t = 0:

∃ infinite B, B + B ⊆ A

Intuitively: if A is 'more than half' of ℕ, the sumset will hit A without needing a shift.

title: Erdős Problem #172
content:
**Erdős Problem #172** is Hindman's theorem itself.

These problems are closely related: #656 is the density analogue of #172.

title: Sárközy's Theorem
content:
**Sárközy's Theorem (1978):**

If A has positive upper density, then A contains two elements differing by a perfect square:

∃ a₁, a₂ ∈ A, ∃ k > 0, a₁ - a₂ = k²

This is another density theorem in the same family as Erdős's conjecture.
mathContext: $\bar{d}(A) > 0 \implies \exists a_1, a_2 \in A,\; \exists k > 0,\; a_1 - a_2 = k^2$

title: Furstenberg Correspondence
content:
The **Furstenberg correspondence principle** translates density statements into ergodic-theoretic ones.

Given A ⊆ ℕ with positive density, there exists a measure-preserving system where:
- Positive density corresponds to positive measure
- Sumset containment corresponds to recurrence

This is the key tool connecting combinatorics to dynamics.

title: Main Result
content:
**Erdős Problem #656: SOLVED**

Answer: YES, every set with positive upper density contains B + B + t for some infinite B and integer t.

The theorem follows from the Kra-Moreira-Richter-Robertson result (2024).

title: Shift is Necessary
content:
**The shift t is sometimes necessary.**

There exist sets A with positive density such that B + B ⊈ A for any infinite B.

Example intuition: Take A to be 'spread out' so that sums always miss certain residue classes.
mathContext: $\exists A$ with $\bar{d}(A) > 0$ such that $\forall B$ infinite, $B + B \not\subseteq A$

title: Quantitative Version
content:
**Quantitative strengthening:**

The infinite set B can be chosen to also have positive density.

This gives a 'density-preserving' version of the theorem.
mathContext: $\bar{d}(A) > 0 \implies \exists B$ infinite with $\bar{d}(B) > 0$ and $\exists t,\; B + B + t \subseteq A$
